amundsen-south-pole-1912-vol2:
Book two of Amundsen's The South Pole came out in 1912. It rounds out his tale of the Fram trip south. The first book told how his team reached the pole in December 1911. This part gives the rest of the trip's work and tale.

A side trip east to King Edward Land and the Fram's long sea cruise fill pages. Notes cover weather, ice, and the life of the far south seas. Amundsen adds full lists of gear and plans that helped the team win. The pair leaves a clear record of a well run polar trip.
anquetil-zend-avesta-vol2:
Tome Two of Anquetil-Duperron's Zend-Avesta, in French from 1771, carries on. The French scholar's bold version of Zoroaster's scriptures fills more rites. His years in India stand behind each hard-won page of text.

Priestly law, purity rules, and hymns to the yazatas fill this tome. Anquetil learned the tongue at Surat from Parsi teachers at first hand. His notes share what those priests told him of their faith. Europe's picture of old Persia's religion grew from efforts like this. The volume keeps the raw thrill of a first encounter alive for readers. Anquetil's daring trip to India stands behind every translated line here.
austin-lectures-jurisprudence-1885-vol2:
Volume Two of Austin's Lectures on Jurisprudence, in Campbell's 1885 edition, applies the command theory across the divisions of law. Austin moves from first principles to the detail of rights, persons, and things. The lectures grow denser as they go.

He treats ownership, contract, injury, and crime under his scheme of primary and sanctioning rights. Roman law supplies many of his examples and terms. Campbell's notes and tables help students through the argument. Together the two volumes complete the system that dominated English legal theory for a century, before critics like Maine and Holmes pushed back against its abstractions.
bayle-miscellaneous-reflections-comet-17:
Volume two carries on Pierre Bayle's Miscellaneous Reflections in the English translation of 1708. The French work first appeared in 1682, after a comet had crossed the sky in December 1680. Bayle, a sharp critic of easy belief, refused to treat that comet as a sign of coming doom.

The second volume presses the same case further against prodigies, oracles, and tales of wonder. Bayle piles up cases from past ages and picks apart the weak proof behind each one. Together, the two volumes form a bold early attack on superstition. They reward readers who like clear reason used with wit.
biruni-india-sachau-1888-vol2:
Sachau's second volume of Alberuni's India, from 1888, completes the great survey begun in the first volume. Al-Biruni turns here to more of India's sciences, festivals, geography, rivers, and daily customs in turn. His method stays the same throughout: report the Hindus' own teaching fairly and fully before judging any part of it.

Few medieval writers crossed cultures with such discipline and such open curiosity about strangers. The two volumes together show a Muslim scholar of about 1030 treating another civilization as worthy of exact, patient study. Sachau's translation, with its learned notes, made that achievement available to the English world, and the pair still anchors Biruni studies.
borlase-dolmens-ireland-1897-vol2:
Book two of Borlase's The Dolmens of Ireland came out in 1897. The set forms the first full survey of the stone tombs of Ireland. This part goes on with the county by county lists. It also spreads the finds out on the map of the land.

Fresh plans show how the tombs were built and how they differ by place. Borlase weighs the spread of the tombs and what that spread may mean. Folk tales and names cling to many of the stones. The book keeps the same close care as the first. It holds facts on sites since harmed or lost.
bracton-note-book-maitland-1887-vol2:
Volume Two of Maitland's Bracton's Note Book prints the case texts themselves. Bracton, a royal justice of the 1200s, had copied real plea-roll cases into his notebook as raw material. Maitland gives them in Latin with his notes.

Disputes over land, inheritance, wardship, and crime crowd the rolls, each one brief and formulaic. Read in bulk, the cases show the young common law at work day by day. Maitland's side notes identify judges, places, and outcomes. This raw judicial material lets readers watch Bracton turn court records into the first great English law treatise.
campbell-popular-tales-west-highlands-18: J. F. Campbell's great set of West Highland tales goes on in this second part, from the same work of 1860. His men took the tales down in Gaelic, word for word, as the folk told them. The set in sum runs to four parts of Highland lore. The tales keep the voice of the tellers of the west coast and isles. Sea lore, seal folk, and the deeds of heroes run through the store Campbell saved.
catlin-letters-and-notes-on-the-north-am:
Catlin's second volume of letters and notes, published with the first in 1841, carries his travels further west and south. It covers the western prairies, the Comanche, and the tribes near the Rocky Mountains that he visited during his journeys of the 1830s.

The letters describe sun dances, medicine rites, horse culture, and hunts on a vast open grassland. Catlin writes as both artist and witness, urging readers to see the worth of the world he was recording. Read with volume one, this book completes one of the most famous early portraits of Native American life on the Plains.
chalmers-further-dialogues-vol2:
Volume Two of Chalmers's Further Dialogues, from 1927, completes his Majjhima Nikaya. The middle-length discourses run to their close in this second half. Kings, monks, and doubters all test the Buddha in talk.

Argument, parable, and gentle irony mark the Buddha's manner here. He probes pride, fear, and the hunger for a lasting self. Long talks build step by step toward calm, clear release. Chalmers keeps his English stately and plain across the whole set. The two volumes give the Majjhima a firm, historic English home at last. Their talks reward readers who take them slowly, one by one.
coke-reports-1777-vol2:
Wilson's 1777 edition of Coke's Reports continued with a second volume of cases from Elizabethan and Jacobean England. Coke reported the decisions of the highest courts, many of them his own, in the age when the common law was taking its modern shape. The Reports as a whole became the most cited case books in English law.

Volume 2 works through disputes over land, contracts, and the powers of courts and crown. Each report is a small lesson in legal growth, as old rules meet new facts and are argued into new form. Coke's voice runs through the commentary, confident and learned. For lawyers of Wilson's day, these volumes were working tools. For historians now, they preserve the living law of Stuart England as its chief maker understood it.
cook-voyage-south-pole-1777-vol2:
Book two of Cook's account of his second voyage came out in 1777. The voyage ran from 1772 to 1775 in the ships Resolution and Adventure. Cook wrote the official tale himself. This part takes the ships deep into the far south seas.

Ice closes round the ships as Cook probes for a southern land and finds none. The tale tells of a stop at Easter Island and its great stone heads. Storms split the two ships, and Cook sails on alone. The book ends the tale of the voyage that redrew the map of the south.
dalrymple-historical-collection-1771-vol:
Book two of Alexander Dalrymple's set of south Pacific voyages came out in 1771. Dalrymple was a sea chart maker who backed the claim of a great southern land. The set prints old logs, charts, and reports from past trips. Cook's voyages were then putting the claim to the test.

More tales of finds in the south seas fill these pages, with notes on winds, isles, and coasts. Dalrymple adds his own views on trade and on lands yet to be found. The two books form the last full plea for Terra Australis. Soon Cook's own logs would end the long debate.
degroot-religious-system-china-vol2:
Volume Two of de Groot's Religious System appeared in 1894 in English. The soul and the world past death take the center here. Ghosts, gods, and the vast ranks of the underworld fill its pages.

De Groot maps the Chinese spirit world like a state with offices. Judges of the dead, clerks, and guards run its grim courts. Tales, rites, and temple lore back his ordered, detailed scheme. His deep learning unfolds the unseen half of Chinese life. Readers gain a guide to beliefs that shaped daily acts for millions of people. The underworld he maps mirrors the earthly state in telling ways.
domat-civil-law-1850-vol2:
Volume Two of Domat's Civil Law in its Natural Order completes Cushing's 1850 edition of Strahan's translation. Domat's plan carries the civil law from contracts into the rules of inheritance. The second volume is the practical half of the system.

Successions, wills, obligations, and the rules of public law occupy these pages. Domat tests each Roman rule against reason and Christian morals, keeping what fits his order. Pothier and then the Code Napoleon drew heavily on this groundwork. Cushing's notes tie the French text to American practice. The two volumes together show Roman law rebuilt as a clear, modern system.
duran-historia-indias-vol2:
Volume 2 of Durán's Historia, from the 1867 first edition, turns to Aztec rites. The Dominican friar sets out the old religion's daily workings in depth. The Aztec calendar and its feasts receive full, patient treatment here.

Durán grew up among Nahua speakers, and it shows on each page. He explains prayers, offerings, and temple routine as an insider's guide. Myths of the gods stand beside notes on food, dress, and custom. The book pairs well with Sahagún's great history of the same world. Together they keep a lost faith's daily life clear for later ages.
dutt-agni-purana-vol2:
Volume 2 of Dutt's Agni Puranam, from 1904, turns to the great arts. Poetry and its rules stand near the front of this part. Grammar, medicine, and the reading of omens fill the wide survey.

Old India's whole course of useful learning passes in one sweep. How verse works, how words form, and how healers treat ills unfold. Kings and scholars alike were meant to master this shared stock. Dutt's English makes the dense old curriculum clear to modern readers. The volume shows the purana at its most handbook-like and broadly useful. Students of Sanskrit letters will find its poetics chapters of real worth.
dutt-garuda-purana-vol2:
Volume 2 of Dutt's Garuda Puranam, from 1908, holds the famed Pretakalpa. The soul's journey after death stands at the center of this part. Judgment of the dead and the rites owed them fill its pages.

Readers learn what meets the soul on the road to Yama's realm. Funeral rites, gifts for the dead, and the fruits of good deeds follow. Families in India have turned to these chapters in grief for ages. The text ranks as the classic Hindu account of the afterlife. Dutt's English carries the solemn teachings in full, calm detail throughout. Few parts of any purana have been read so often in private grief.
frazer-totemism-and-exogamy-1910-vol2:
The second volume of Frazer's 1910 treatise carries his survey of totemism across three continents. Volume one set out the scheme of totem clans and marriage rules; this one tests it against Australia, Africa, and the Americas.

Frazer works through tribe after tribe, comparing clan names, food taboos, and myths of descent from the totem. Australian evidence, the richest of all, takes a large share. He weighs rival theories of how such systems begin and spread. Modern anthropology later rejected much of Frazer's method, but the mass of collected fact in these volumes is still mined by researchers today.
freneau-poems-1907-vol2:
Volume two of Pattee's Freneau carries the poet past the war years and into the new republic. Like the first volume, it was printed at Princeton by the University Library in 1903. The contents continue the full sweep of a long and combative writing life.

Freneau struck at Federalists in sharp satire and praised American scenes in lyric verse. He also wrote some of the first American poems on Native peoples and the western frontier. His nature lyrics can feel strikingly fresh even now. The range on show is that of a poet and newsman who never stopped fighting with his pen.
grimm-teutonic-mythology-1882-vol2: Jacob Grimm's vast study of German myth goes on in this second part, in Stallybrass's English text. The whole work in English runs to four parts, drawn from Grimm's German text. Grimm built it from poems, laws, tales, and the speech of the folk. The survey moves from the gods to the rites, beings, and beliefs round them. Each claim rests on a heap of quotes from old texts in many tongues.
hahnemann-materia-medica-pura-dudgeon-18:
Dudgeon's second volume of Hahnemann's Materia Medica Pura appeared at London in 1881, completing the two-volume English edition. It carries the provings from Ledum through Verbascum, the second half of Hahnemann's alphabet of remedies. Richard Hughes's annotations continue beside Dudgeon's translation, as in volume one.

Each proving records, symptom by symptom, what the substance stirred in healthy testers. Hahnemann meant the records as the sole safe basis for prescribing by similars. Together the Dudgeon volumes gave English homeopaths their founder's core data unabridged. The set remains in print among practitioners more than a century later. Readers of medical history meet here the primary text of homeopathy's first school. Precision, not theory, is its ruling manner.
holdsworth-history-english-law-1922-vol2:
Volume Two of Holdsworth's History, in the 1922 third edition, covers Anglo-Saxon and Norman law and the sources of English law. With the courts mapped in Volume One, Holdsworth turns to the materials themselves. His plan is slow, vast, and exact.

He examines the dooms, the charters, the plea rolls, and the treatises from Glanvill to Bracton and beyond. The Norman settlement's effect on English custom gets careful, balanced treatment. Holdsworth also weighs the Year Books and the early reports as evidence. The volume is a guide to the records every legal historian must master, written by a master of them all.
hose-mcdougall-the-pagan-tribes-of-borne:
Hose and McDougall devoted the second volume of their 1912 Borneo study to religion and magic among the peoples of the island's interior. The first volume covered daily life and social order; this one asks what the Kayan, Kenyah, and their neighbors believed about souls, spirits, and the unseen world.

Readers find accounts of shamans and healing rites, beliefs about the soul's travels after death, and the role of omens in daily choices. Headhunting ritual and the cult of the omen birds receive long, careful treatment. The volume closes a work still valued as one of the fullest early records of Borneo belief.
husserl-logische-untersuchungen-1900-vol:
The second volume of Husserl's Logical Investigations followed the first in 1900, both in German. Where volume 1 attacked psychologism, volume 2 builds the positive theory. It holds the six investigations that made Husserl's name and seeded the phenomenological movement.

The studies ask what meaning is, how words carry it, and how the mind aims at objects through its acts. Husserl sorts the parts and wholes of experience and describes how evidence feels when a claim is truly fulfilled. The close study of consciousness unfolds here in full, years before he named the method behind it. Readers from several schools, analytic as well as continental, have mined the volume. It stands as the founding text of the century's most fertile school of thought.
johnson-dictionary-english-language-1755:
Volume Two of Johnson's Dictionary covers the letters L through Z, completing the 1755 work in its 1756 second-edition form. Johnson had done the work of whole academies with a handful of helpers. The second volume carries the same mix of rigor and personality.

Definitions draw on quotations from Shakespeare, Milton, and Dryden to fix each sense. Johnson also marks words as low, barbarous, or dying, acting as judge as well as recorder. Together the two volumes fixed English spelling and meaning for generations. Modern dictionaries still stand in the shadow of Johnson's plan and prose.
junod-life-south-african-tribe-1913-vol2:
Junod's second volume, The Psychic Life, followed in 1913 and turns from Thonga society to Thonga belief. Ancestor worship stands at the center, with magic, divination, possession, and the spirit world around it. Henri Alexandre Junod gathered the material across decades beside the people of Mozambique and the Transvaal.

Rites for the dead, medicines with souls, and gods of sky and family all get patient, detailed treatment. Read with the social volume, the pair gives a whole civilization from inside and outside at once. The Psychic Life completes one of the great works of early anthropology.
king-seven-tablets-creation-1902-vol2:
Volume two of King's Seven Tablets of Creation, published in 1902, is the supplementary volume to his Enuma Elish edition. It prints newly published Neo-Babylonian cuneiform texts of the Creation series as autographed plates. An English preface and tablet-by-tablet descriptions guide readers through the copies.

The plates let Assyriologists check King's readings sign by sign against the clay. Some tablets add lines and variants that sharpen the epic's text in volume one. Such apparatus made the edition a working tool, not only a translation. King's two volumes together introduced the Babylonian creation epic to English scholarship in full. They record a moment when cuneiform studies were young and fast-growing. The series' texts have been re-edited since, on King's foundations.
lafitau-moeurs-sauvages-vol2:
Volume 2 of Lafitau's Moeurs, in French from 1724, carries his great comparison further. Religion, government, and the art of war stand at the center here. Each Iroquois practice is set against Greek and Roman parallels from old texts.

Lafitau hunts for what all peoples share beneath their differences of place. Councils, war parties, and rites unfold in patient, learned detail. His years in Canada ground the book's bold claims in lived fact. The work ranks among the most fresh and bold books of its century. It remains a Jesuit's search for the shared roots of human custom.
lamb-works-lucas-vol2:
Charles Lamb wrote his most famous work under the pen name Elia, and Lucas gathered those essays in this second volume of 1903. The contents list The South-Sea House first, then Oxford in the Vacation and Christ's Hospital. Dream-Children, one of his best-known pieces, appears later in the book.

Warm, funny, and often sad, the essays dwell on London life, old books, whist, and lost friends. Pieces like The Two Races of Men and Mrs. Battle's Opinions on Whist show his playful side. Readers have loved them for two centuries because they feel like letters from a witty and tender friend.
langland-piers-plowman-wright-1887-vol2:
Volume II of Wright's 1887 Piers Plowman completes the standard edition of Langland's dream-vision. The search that began in a field of folk deepens here toward Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest, the stages of the good life. Langland revised his poem across his life, and the latter dreams grow stranger and more searching.

Piers the plowman, first met as a humble guide, takes on a near-sacred role by the end. The dreamer's hunt for a true life becomes a judgment on the church of his day. Together the two Wright volumes gave generations of readers their Langland, the fierce, tender voice of medieval England.
las-casas-historia-indias-vol2:
Volume 2 of the Historia de las Indias appeared in the Madrid edition of 1875. Las Casas follows Columbus on his later voyages across the Atlantic. First settlements rise in the islands as Spanish rule takes firm hold.

A grim pattern forms in these chapters, year by hard year. Greed drives forced labor, raids, and the ruin of Native towns. Las Casas builds his case with names, dates, and sworn detail. He had lived in the colonies and knew the men involved. The great defender's vast case against the conquest gains weight and shape here.
marston-works-bullen-1887-vol2:
Volume two of A. H. Bullen's 1887 edition carries John Marston's work into his best-known plays. The title page and contents list The Dutch Courtesan first, followed by The Fawn and The Wonder of Women, also called The Tragedy of Sophonisba. Marston wrote for the London stage in the early 1600s.

Across these plays, comedy and tragedy share the same sharp eye for greed, lust, and court intrigue. The Dutch Courtesan in particular became one of his most acted works. Together the pieces show why crowds both loved and feared his pen, and why his name still stands for biting Jacobean satire.
mawson-home-blizzard-1915-vol2:
Book two of Mawson's The Home of the Blizzard came out in 1915. It ends his tale of the Australasian trip from 1911 to 1914. The first book told of the wild winds at Cape Denison and of Mawson's lone walk back. This part gives the work of the other bases.

Teams at the far west base and on Macquarie Island tell their own tales. Reports cover rocks, ice, weather, and the life of the south seas. The ship Aurora threads the whole tale with its trips through pack ice. The pair forms the full record of a vast, harsh trip.
meyer-nutt-voyage-bran-1895-vol2:
Book two of Meyer and Nutt's Voyage of Bran came out in 1895. The first book gave the Irish text of Bran's sea trip to the Land of the Living. This book turns to what the old Celts held on the soul. Nutt leads the study side of the work.

The Celts held that the soul is born again in new flesh, Nutt argues. He draws on Welsh and Irish tales to make the case in full. Notes set the Bran tale beside like tales from other lands. The pair of books still forms the base set for the tale.
middleton-works-dyce-1840-vol2:
Volume Two of Dyce's 1840 Middleton continues the collected plays of the Jacobean dramatist. Dyce worked from the earliest prints, correcting and annotating as he went. The edition aimed to give scholars a sound text and readers a lost author back.

Middleton's city comedies shine in this part of the set: London merchants, gallants, and cheats move through plots of debt and desire. His ear for the speech of shops and streets was unmatched in his age. The tragedies among them turn the same wit to darker ends. Reading the volume shows why modern stages have taken Middleton up again with such hunger.
neumann-reden-gotamo-buddhos-vol2:
Neumann's German Majjhima Nikaya continues in the second volume of Die Reden Gotamo Buddhos, dated 1921 like its mates. The Mittlere Sammlung, the middle collection of the Buddha's discourses, runs long, and this band carries its central stretch. Karl Eugen Neumann translated the Pali with a poet's ear and a scholar's care for the sense.

Similes of rafts, fires, and arrows carry teachings on craving, self, and release from suffering. Lay readers in German lands met the Buddha's own voice here rather than summaries written about him by others. The volume holds the middle of a set that founded Buddhist reading in Germany.
pollock-maitland-history-english-law-189:
Volume Two of Pollock and Maitland, also 1895, sets out the doctrines of the common law down to 1272. Where the first volume tells the story, this one explains the rules. Tenure, courts, procedure, crime, and tort receive full treatment.

The authors show a law still fluid, feeling its way toward forms that would last centuries. Marriage, inheritance, and the law of villeins reveal a whole society inside the doctrine. Maitland's chapters on crime and tort are models of the craft. Completing the 1895 first edition, this volume made the set the fixed starting point for all study of medieval English law.
radloff-aus-sibirien-1893-vol2:
Volume two of Radloff's Aus Sibirien, in the Leipzig second edition of 1893, continues his Siberian journals in German. The leaves here gather further shamanic and ethnographic material from the Altai and the Kirghiz steppe. Radloff records rites, burials, epics, and daily crafts as he met them between 1859 and 1870.

A table of Russian measures closes the volume, a traveler's tool of the period. Radloff's ear for language shapes everything: names, songs, and terms are set down exactly. Later ethnographers built on his Siberian record for a century. The two volumes together form one of the great travel archives of inner Asia. They reward readers who like their wonders documented, not embellished.
rattray-hausa-folklore-vol2:
Volume Two of Rattray's Hausa Folk-Lore followed in the same year, 1913. More tales, proverbs, and customs extend his Northern Nigeria gathering. The people's own words carry the book, in Hausa and in English.

Daily life in the Hausa cities fills these pages in fine detail. Marriage, trade, law, and jest all find their place in the tales. Rattray's ear for the spoken word keeps the tellers' voices warm. The pair of volumes counts as pioneer work in African studies. Readers gain both fine stories and a true record of a living culture. The second volume deepens the first without repeating its best tales.
rhys-celtic-folklore-1901-vol2: John Rhys ends his set of Welsh and Manx folk lore with this second part, the mate to the first of 1901. The set as a whole is his 1901 work in two parts. Rhys spent years on the folk lore of Wales and the Isle of Man. The second part rounds out the store of fairy and ghost lore. Sea lore from both lands runs through the set, from Welsh lakes to Manx shores. With the first, it forms the main book on the lore of Wales and Man.
rivers-the-history-of-melanesian-society:
The second volume of Rivers's 1914 Melanesian history turns from rites and societies to kinship. Where volume one traced migrations through custom, this one works through the words Melanesian peoples use for relatives, treating those systems as fossils of past social life.

Rivers compares kinship terminologies island by island and argues they record older forms of marriage and descent. From these he rebuilds a sequence of social change across the Pacific. The reasoning is intricate and much of it has not survived later research. Even so, the volume shows the era's faith that careful comparison could recover history without documents.
ross-voyage-southern-seas-1847-vol2:
Book two of Ross's tale of the Erebus and Terror trip came out in 1847. The trip ran from 1839 to 1843 under James Clark Ross. These pages take the ships through their last south seasons. The first book told of the Ross Sea and the ice shelf.

Fresh probes into the pack, new charts, and hard ice work fill the tale. Ross writes of the crews' health, the ships' state, and the slow sail home. Notes on birds, fish, and ice forms add worth for men of science. The pair of books forms the full record of a landmark voyage.
sahagun-historia-general-vol2:
Volume 2 of Sahagún's General History appeared in Bustamante's 1829 printing in Spanish. The book sets out the Aztec calendar and its round of feasts. Omens that ruled Nahua life get full and careful treatment here.

Native informants describe the sacred year feast by feast, month by month. They explain signs, dreams, and the gods honored at each turn. Sahagún records their words with patience and rare respect for detail. The result is a treasury of a worldview then being destroyed. Readers meet the Aztec year as its own people lived and feared it. Few books bring that lost rhythm so close.
scott-last-expedition-1913-vol2:
Book two of Scott's Last Expedition came out in 1913. The first book held Scott's own journals of the Terra Nova trip. This book gives the reports of the other teams and the men of science. The trip ran from 1910 to 1913.

Side trips to far coasts, rock hunts, and a winter in an ice cave fill the reports. Notes cover ice, weather, birds, and sea life in fine grain. The book shows the trip was more than a race for the pole. Its science gave facts that polar study used for years.
scott-voyage-discovery-1905-vol2:
Book two of Scott's Voyage of the Discovery came out in 1905. It ends his tale of the British trip south from 1901 to 1904. The first book told of the first winter and the far south sled trip. This part covers the last year and the sail home.

More sled trips cross the ice shelf and climb the inland hills. Scott tells of relief ships that freed the Discovery from the ice at last. Notes on the land, the ice, and the life found there fill the close. The pair fixed Scott's fame as a polar leader.
shackleton-heart-antarctic-1909-vol2:
Book two of Shackleton's Heart of the Antarctic came out in 1909. It completes his tale of the Nimrod trip of 1907 to 1909. The first book told of the pole dash and the climb of Mount Erebus. This part gives the rest of the work in the field.

Reports from the side parties fill much of the book, with notes on rocks, ice, and life. Maps and charts show the routes the sled teams took. Shackleton adds lists of gear, food, and stores used on the trip. The two books form the full tale of the trip that made his name.
skeat-blagden-pagan-races-of-the-malay-p:
Skeat and Blagden published the second volume of their survey of the Malay Peninsula's pagan races in 1906, the same year as the first. Where volume one covered bodies and daily life, this one turns to religion, folklore, and language among the Semang, Sakai, and Jakun.

Inside are accounts of shamans and their seances, beliefs about the soul, charms, spells, and the magic used against sickness and harm. The authors also record myths, tales, and word lists gathered from the people themselves. For readers, the volume preserves beliefs and speech that were already fading under outside pressure, told in unusual depth for its time.
smith-dale-ila-speaking-vol2:
Edwin Smith and Andrew Dale issued Volume Two on the Ila-speaking peoples in 1920. Their study of Northern Rhodesia's Ba-ila counts as a classic record. Religion, magic, and social order fill this second volume's pages.

Smith and Dale knew the people well from years of shared life. They record rites, beliefs, and rules with rare depth and care. Gods, spirits, and the bonds of clan and village stand clear. The pair of volumes forms the fullest early account of its kind. Readers gain a Central African world rendered in its own terms here. Volume One, held elsewhere in the catalog, completes the matched pair.
story-commentaries-constitution-1833-vol:
Volume Two of Story's Commentaries, also 1833, turns from history to the Constitution itself. Story takes up the legislature, the executive, and the powers of Congress clause by clause. His aim was to teach the republic its own frame of government.

He defends a strong but limited federal power, reading the necessary and proper clause broadly. Story's views on the presidency and the veto remain instructive today. The volume's calm, teacherly tone hides firm Federalist convictions. Generations of lawyers and judges learned the Constitution from Story before they read the cases, and many still rate him its finest early expositor.
tennyson-poems-1842-vol2:
Alfred Tennyson's two-volume Poems of 1842 ended his long retreat after bad reviews and set him on the road to the laureateship. This second volume completes the collection. It leans more toward English scenes and story poems than its companion volume.

Readers find narrative pieces, lyrics, and dramatic sketches in Tennyson's polished early manner. Poems of rural life and memory sit beside classical and romantic tales. The craftsmanship that critics had mocked a decade earlier now looks like mastery. Together the two volumes form the true starting point of Tennyson's career, the base from which In Memoriam and the Idylls grew.
thorpe-ancient-laws-england-1840-vol2:
Volume Two of Thorpe's Ancient Laws and Institutes, also 1840, completes the Record Commission edition. It holds the later Anglo-Saxon and Anglo-Norman legal texts that follow the early kings' codes. Thorpe adds a glossary and full indexes.

Church laws, guild rules, and the laws once ascribed to Edward the Confessor and William the Conqueror fill this volume. The texts show English law absorbing Norman rule and Latin forms. Thorpe's glossary unlocks the Old English legal terms for students. Together the two volumes give the raw material from which the common law grew, in one scholarly set.
thorpe-northern-mythology-1851-vol2:
Benjamin Thorpe, an English scholar of the north, made this great set of the folk tales of Scandinavia in 1851. The second part came out the same year as the first. Thorpe drew on Danish, Swedish, and Norse stores of tales told by the folk.

The tales here hold the lore of the merman and the mermaid of the cold seas. Sea folk who wed men, sing on rocks, and drag ships down fill these pages with dread and charm. The set is a chief source in English for the sea lore of the north.
webster-american-dictionary-1828-vol2:
Volume Two of Webster's 1828 American Dictionary completes the first edition, running through the second half of the alphabet. Webster had sold his earlier spelling books by the million to pay for this work. He saw the dictionary as a school for the whole nation.

The definitions favor clarity and moral order, and the roots reach back through Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. Webster hoped a shared language would bind the states into one people. Printers and teachers took the book up at once. With this volume, the founding work of American lexicography stands complete. Teachers in one-room schools taught spelling straight from its pages.
wolfram-parzival-weston-1894-vol2:
Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival is the fullest medieval telling of the Grail quest. Jessie Weston's English translation appeared in two volumes, and this second one, from 1894, covers Books Ten through Sixteen. It takes up the hero after his great failure at the Grail castle.

Parzival wanders for years in doubt and despair, angry at God and at himself. The hermit Trevrizent explains the Grail's mystery and his own family's part in it. Slowly the hero grows fit for a second chance. He returns to the castle at last, asks the question he once swallowed, and takes up the Grail kingship.
wordsworth-lyrical-ballads-1800-vol2:
William Wordsworth's second volume of the 1800 Lyrical Ballads holds the new poems he wrote for the expanded edition. The first volume carried his famous Preface. This one lets the poetry speak, and it contains some of his most loved work.

Michael, a long blank-verse tale, tells of an old shepherd who loses his son and his land after a lifetime of labor. The Brothers gives another tale of rural loss around a churchyard. The short Lucy poems mourn a young woman who lived unknown and died early. Hart-Leap Well and other ballads round out the volume. These poems fixed Wordsworth's plain, deep style in readers' minds.
wright-narratives-of-sorcery-and-magic-1:
Thomas Wright's second volume of Narratives of Sorcery and Magic appeared in 1851 beside the first. It completes his Victorian history of witchcraft drawn from authentic sources. The antiquary's narrative method continues: let the records tell the story, with his learning as the thread between them.

The later and bloodier centuries take the stage here. Famous trials, confessions, and executions unfold from the documents themselves. Wright keeps his tone lively even in grim matter. Together the two volumes gave general readers a documented history of magic and persecution. His work shaped how the nineteenth century pictured the witch era, as a closed past of folly overcome by reason.
